stops.title: Where to type
stops.text:
Type your search in this box, in the panel on the left: a label, then the word forms. Here the label is *Tasalṭana* and `\w*tslTn\w*` is the search. Arabic letters work too.
Then press *Search*.

stops.title: The forms found
stops.text:
`\w*` means “any letters”, so the search catches every form built on *tslTn*: *tasalṭana*, *wa-tasalṭana*, *yatasalṭanu*, and also *al-mutasalṭin*.
This list is where you select the forms: tick or untick each one, or use *tick all* and *untick all*.

stops.title: Untick a form
stops.text:
Each form has a tick box. Here *al-mutasalṭin* is unticked, so the results now count 11 of the 12 forms.
Untick any form you don't want and press *Update results*, and every chart and table follows.

stops.title: Over time
stops.text:
*Tasalṭana* means “to become sultan”. The curve shows its share of all words in each 25-year period.
It is almost absent until the eighth century AH, well into the Mamlūk period, and peaks in the ninth century AH.

stops.title: Raw counts and corpus size
stops.text:
These are the raw counts. The grey bars show how much text the corpus holds for each period.
A rise can simply mean more surviving texts — which is why the relative view is the default.

stops.title: Books
stops.text: Which books use the word, and how often. A handful of works account for much of it.

stops.title: Authors
stops.text: Roughly a third of all uses are in the works of Ibn Taġrībirdī (d. 874/1470).

stops.title: Book types, compared with corpus
stops.text:
Is the word typical of a kind of book? Chronicles use it far more than their share of the corpus predicts.
The box above the chart explains how to read it.

stops.title: Your turn
stops.text:
Click any book or author to open its profile in the Book Classifier.
Use “Copy link” or “Cite these results” to keep exactly this view.
